readme.markdown:
# Ekwo OS

**Ekwo** is open source accounting, ready to use on **[Ekwo Cloud](https://cloud.ekwo.ai)**: the web application for your invoices, your bank statements, your VAT returns and the electronic invoices your country uses, in your own instance, with an account opened in a minute. **Ekwo OS** is the free and open source core it runs on, under AGPL-3.0: install it on your own Supabase project and own your accounting data, forever.

Built and maintained by **Ekwo**. Ekwo OS is a schema, the rules of each country as data, and the tools — a command line and an MCP server — with which you, your accountant and the AI agent you choose work in the same books, each with their own access. Ekwo reads any supplier invoice, in any language, with the AI model you choose, and every entry is posted on your confirmation. What Ekwo is, and its limits: [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md).

*From an empty Supabase project to a prepared VAT return, for two countries
side by side. How it was recorded: [`docs/demo/`](docs/demo/).*

**Try it on your own books.** Already using Claude? [Start with
Claude](docs/start-with-claude.md) goes from a free Supabase project to your
own books taken over, questioned and your next VAT return prepared, in about
twenty minutes. Or open the same books in the web application,
[Ekwo Cloud](https://cloud.ekwo.ai).

---

## Why Ekwo

> The long version — financial autonomy for every business, accounting as a
> commons, a network rather than a vendor — is in [MANIFESTO.md](MANIFESTO.md).

**The data belongs to the business, and the work of keeping the books can be
done by software the business also owns.** So the whole accounting core is
open, the data sits in a Postgres database you control, and the interface is
designed for machines as much as for people. Supabase gives the schema a REST
API for free, and an MCP server sits on top of it, so an AI agent can book a
purchase, match a payment or prepare a VAT return on your own data — as you,
under your own row level security, without the data leaving your account.

What ships today:

- **The core** — schema, posting rules, taxes, reports, financial statements,
  as migrations you apply to a database you control.
- **A country pack for every country listed below**, each a versioned set of
  data with a year of books that proves it.
- **`ekwo`, the command line** — one command installs everything on your own
  Supabase project; the same tool then keeps books from a terminal.
- **The MCP server**, hosted at `https://mcp.ekwo.ai/mcp` or run locally with
  `npx @ekwo-ai/mcp`, so any AI agent can operate the books.
- **Modules** for fixed assets, budgets, corporate income tax and electronic
  invoicing.
- **The compass of the company** — `financial_analysis()` reads, from the
  posted entries, the aggregates a country pack defines (revenue, equity,
  cash, receivables, payables…), or, in a country whose pack defines none,
  thirteen of them read by account type through the generic framework, so that days of cash, net margin, current
  ratio, equity ratio, days of sales and of purchases outstanding and growth
  come from the books with nothing to set up. The Analysis screen of Ekwo
  Cloud and the `financial_analysis` tool of the MCP server read it;
  [`docs/analysis.md`](docs/analysis.md) says how, and how a pack adds the
  section.
- **Format libraries** under MIT — the files administrations, banks and
  e-invoicing networks exchange, written and read.

Who it is for: a company that wants to keep its own books with an AI at the
keyboard, and a founder who wants to know, from those books, how long the cash
lasts and how fast customers pay; an accounting firm that runs several
companies inside one installation; a developer who needs a real double-entry
core with tax rules as data rather than as code; and anyone who wants to leave
a proprietary system with the books intact.

## What is in this repository

A double-entry accounting core for Postgres. There is no server to run:
Supabase turns the schema into a REST API with an OpenAPI description, and row
level security decides who sees what.

- **Double entry, enforced by the database.** An entry cannot be posted unless
  it balances, and a locked period refuses writes at the trigger — not in a
  form validator.
- **Documents and entries are two layers.** An invoice answers to EN 16931 and
  Peppol; an entry answers to the chart of accounts. Keeping them apart keeps
  both honest.
- **Country rules are data.** A tax points at the ledger accounts it posts to
  and at the boxes of the declaration it feeds. Adding a régime is a row, not a
  release.
- **Every label is data, in every language a country pack publishes.**
  Identifiers stay English; what a person reads comes from the pack, in the
  language of the company or of the reader. See
  [`docs/languages.md`](docs/languages.md).
- **Every country a pack, out of the box.** United Arab Emirates (`ae`), Antigua and Barbuda (`ag`), Albania (`al`), Հայաստան (`am`), Angola (`ao`), Argentina (`ar`), Austria (`at`), Australia (`au`), Azərbaycan (`az`), Bosna i Hercegovina (`ba`), Barbados (`bb`), Bangladesh (`bd`), Belgium (`be`), Burkina Faso (`bf`), България (`bg`), البحرين (`bh`), Burundi (`bi`), Bénin (`bj`), Bermuda (`bm`), Brunei Darussalam (`bn`), Bolivia (`bo`), Brasil (`br`), The Bahamas (`bs`), Bhutan (`bt`), Botswana (`bw`), Canada (`ca`), République démocratique du Congo (`cd`), Centrafrique (`cf`), Congo (`cg`), Schweiz (`ch`), Côte d’Ivoire (`ci`), Chile (`cl`), Cameroun (`cm`), 中国 (`cn`), Colombia (`co`), Costa Rica (`cr`), Cabo Verde (`cv`), Cyprus (`cy`), Czechia (`cz`), Germany (`de`), Djibouti (`dj`), Danmark (`dk`), Dominica (`dm`), Dominican Republic (`do`), Algérie (`dz`), Ecuador (`ec`), Estonia (`ee`), مصر (`eg`), España (`es`), Ethiopia (`et`), Finland (`fi`), Fiji (`fj`), France (`fr`), Gabon (`ga`), United Kingdom (`gb`), Grenada (`gd`), საქართველო (`ge`), Guernsey (`gg`), Ghana (`gh`), The Gambia (`gm`), Guinée (`gn`), G

name: ai-browser
description: Visible Electron browser driven by a semantic accessibility tree: 17 MCP tools, no screenshots.

readme.markdown: AI Browser 中文读者请看这里：README-CN.md（3 分钟速读 + 中文安装指引） A real browser whose only operator is your agent. It reads pages as a semantic tree instead of screenshots, acts through trusted browser input — and because it is a normal, visible Electron window, a human can reach for the mouse at any time. A noisy real-world feed (300+ accessibility nodes) becomes a typed structure — then one ui.act switches the feed and the tree changes with it. Every call is a raw JSON-RPC message over one WebSocket: no SDK, no coordinates. Reproduce: npm start then node examples/feed-tree.mjs Human + agent, same browser, same socket. The agent drives, then simply stops and watches; a person clicks an article in the real window, the agent notices the new tab on its next read, and continues on the page the human chose. No lock, no hand-off API. Try it yourself: npm start then node examples/human-takeover.mjs — click anything when it says YOUR TURN. **What it is.** An Electron app that exposes its tabs over two equivalent interfaces — an MCP server (20 `browse_*` tools) and a raw WebSocket JSON-RPC API (`ws://localhost:9223`, methods `ui.*`). Your agent navigates, reads a structured semantic tree (`role` / `label` / `value` / `states` / `actions`), and clicks or types by `data-ai-id`. There is no screenshot step and no OCR: `src/` contains no capture call at all. **What it is not.** It is not headless. The window really opens, really renders, and stays interactive — see [Letting a human step in](#letting-a-human-step-in). Nor does it "co-drive" with you: the hand-off is a conversation between the agent and the user, not a browser API. > **Security note.** The WebSocket server has no authentication — it listens on localhost and trusts > whoever connects. Do not expose port 9223 beyond loopback, and avoid untrusted networks. --- ## Install **Install the prebuilt package unless you have a reason not to.** Option A is one file you double-click: no Node.js, no dependency tree, no build step. Source install (Option C) pulls a ~276 MB `node_modules` plus a ~100 MB Electron engine download on top — only use it when no package fits your platform, the package misbehaves, or you specifically need to run from source. ### Option A — macOS install package (recommended) Grab `AI-Browser--arm64.dmg` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Glittering/ai-browser/releases) (~110 MB to download, ~245 MB on disk — most of it is the bundled Chromium engine, which *is* the product). Open the dmg, drag **AI Browser** to `/Applications`, launch it. Done. Two things to know before you download it: - **It is not notarized.** macOS Gatekeeper will refuse to open it on the first try. Right-click the app → **Open**, confirm once, and it runs normally afterwards. (A paid Apple Developer account is what removes this step; until then, this is the honest cost.) - **Only macOS `arm64` is built.** Windows and Linux have no package yet, because neither has been verified on this project — see [Compatibility](#compatibility). Agents still connect through the MCP server (Option B below), and the two channels cooperate: when the packaged app is already running, the MCP server finds it on port 9223 and **reuses it instead of spawning a second copy of Electron** — one browser, one login session, whichever way you start it. So "package for the engine + `npx` for the MCP bridge" is the normal agent setup too. ### Option B — npx (the agent channel) The package is published as [`@glittering0717/ai-browser`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@glittering0717/ai-browser); no clone needed: ```bash npx -y @glittering0717/ai-browser --help ``` To open the visible browser window directly: ```bash npx -y @glittering0717/ai-browser start ``` Requires **Node ≥ 18** and a desktop session (this is a GUI app). If a launch needs its own engine, the first run prepares it (~100 MB, downloaded once). npm ≥ 11 blocks dependency install scripts by default — the launcher detects that and runs Electron's own downloader itself, so nothing extra is needed. If the download from GitHub releases is slow or blocked (common on mainland-China networks), point it at a mirror: ```bash ELECTRON_MIRROR=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/ npx -y @glittering0717/ai-browser start ``` ### Option C — from source (fallback) Use this when there is no package for your platform, the package gives you trouble, or you need to modify the code. It is the heaviest of the three: `npm install` pulls the full dependency tree (~276 MB), then the Electron engine (~100 MB) on top. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Glittering/ai-browser.git cd ai-browser npm install ``` If the Electron binary download is slow or fails outright, use the mirror: ```bash ELECTRON_MIRROR=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/ npm install ``` Or make it sticky by creating a `.npmrc` in the project root: ```ini electron_mirror=https://npmmirror.com/mirrors/electron/ ``` Confirm the binary actually landed before blaming anything else — a missing binary still leaves you with an "install that succeeded": ```bash ls node_modules/electron/dist ``` To check the install end to end: ```bash npm start ``` A 1280×800 window opens and the terminal prints `AI Browser WS server listening on ws://localhost:9223`. (The first tab opens on the default start page; ignore it and navigate away.) To build the package yourself: ```bash npm install node scripts/build_dmg.cjs # current arch node scripts/build_dmg.cjs --arch arm64 # or x64 ``` Output lands in `dist/`. The script uses `@electron/packager` plus macOS's built-in `hdiutil` (no external binary downloads); the reasoning — including why `electron-builder` refuses to build this project — is documented in [`docs/DEPENDENCY_AND_DISTRIBUTION_AUDIT.md`](docs/DEPENDENCY_AND_DISTRIBUTION_AUDIT.md). …

readme.markdown:
# atlassian-browser-mcp

MCP server that wraps the upstream [mcp-atlassian](https://github.com/sooperset/mcp-atlassian) toolset with browser-cookie authentication via Playwright, for Atlassian Server/Data Center instances behind corporate SSO (Okta, SAML, etc.) where API tokens are not available. It runs locally over stdio: you log in once with the bundled CLI, and the server reuses the cookies.

## Features

- Every mcp-atlassian Jira and Confluence tool, authenticated with your SSO browser session instead of an API token, with upstream's own network hardening (SSRF redirect checks, DNS pinning, retries, rate limits, proxy and TLS settings) kept in force.
- One login per service with the CLI; the server itself never opens a browser, so it never hangs waiting for one.
- `atlassian_auth_status` tells an agent which service needs a login before it fails mid-task.
- Optional one-time seeding of the automation profile from your real Chrome profile (`ATLASSIAN_SEED_FROM_CHROME_PROFILE`), so the first login is often one click.
- On macOS, reuses a live session from an installed Chromium-family browser (Arc, Brave, Edge, Chrome and others) without opening a window. It reads that browser's Keychain key, says so on stderr, and can be turned off.
- Separate cookie jars for Jira and Confluence, holding only that host's cookies, mode 0600. Jira-only or Confluence-only setups work.
- A command-line front-end (`atlassian-cli`) for scripts and agents: get and search issues and pages.
- Falls back to token auth with `ATLASSIAN_BROWSER_AUTH_ENABLED=false`.

## Quick start

From PyPI, with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) installed:

```bash
JIRA_URL=https://jira.example.com uvx --from atlassian-browser-mcp atlassian-cli login jira   # once per service, opens your browser
CONFLUENCE_URL=https://confluence.example.com uvx --from atlassian-browser-mcp atlassian-cli login confluence
JIRA_URL=https://jira.example.com CONFLUENCE_URL=https://confluence.example.com uvx atlassian-browser-mcp
```

From a checkout, with the exact versions in `uv.lock`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/GeiserX/atlassian-browser-mcp.git && cd atlassian-browser-mcp
UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=.venv-atlassian-browser uv sync --frozen   # installs the versions in uv.lock
JIRA_URL=https://jira.example.com CONFLUENCE_URL=https://confluence.example.com ./atlassian-cli login jira   # once per service
```

Needs Python 3.11+, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Google Chrome and a display for the login. The server never opens a browser window. It reads the saved cookies; when they are missing or expired it returns an `AuthRequiredError` asking you to run the login again, and on macOS it also looks for a live session in your installed browsers in the background, so a retry a few seconds later may already work. Seeding from Chrome and every setting are in [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md).

## Add it to your client

Every client runs the server over stdio. Set only the URL of a service you use. The examples use the PyPI package through `uvx`; from a checkout, replace `uvx atlassian-browser-mcp` with `/path/to/atlassian-browser-mcp/run-atlassian-browser-mcp.sh`.

**Claude Code**

```bash
claude mcp add --transport stdio atlassian \
  --env JIRA_URL=https://jira.example.com \
  --env CONFLUENCE_URL=https://confluence.example.com \
  -- uvx atlassian-browser-mcp
```

**Claude Desktop** (`claude_desktop_config.json`) and **Cursor** (`~/.cursor/mcp.json` or `.cursor/mcp.json`)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "atlassian": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["atlassian-browser-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "JIRA_URL": "https://jira.example.com",
        "CONFLUENCE_URL": "https://confluence.example.com"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**VS Code** (`.vscode/mcp.json`)

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "atlassian": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["atlassian-browser-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "JIRA_URL": "https://jira.example.com",
        "CONFLUENCE_URL": "https://confluence.example.com"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Codex** (`~/.codex/config.toml`)

```toml
[mcp_servers.atlassian]
command = "uvx"
args = ["atlassian-browser-mcp"]
env = { JIRA_URL = "https://jira.example.com", CONFLUENCE_URL = "https://confluence.example.com" }
```

**Protocol.** Speaks MCP 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05 over stdio, which covers clients that open with an `initialize` handshake (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and VS Code today). MCP 2026-07-28 is not supported yet: upstream mcp-atlassian pins `mcp<2` and `fastmcp<4` (https://github.com/sooperset/mcp-atlassian/issues/1541), and this server follows as soon as upstream moves. It runs on stdio only and refuses to start with any other `FASTMCP_TRANSPORT`.

## Read-only mode

Write tools act as you, with your SSO identity. To hide all of them (create, update, delete, transition, upload, restrictions), set `READ_ONLY_MODE=true` in the server's `env`. Upstream enforces it when listing and when calling. `ENABLED_TOOLS` (a comma-separated allow-list of tool names) and `TOOLSETS` narrow the list further; see [Configuration](docs/configuration.md).

## Tools

| Tool | What it does | Hints |
|------|--------------|-------|
| `atlassian_auth_status` | Whether each service's saved session exists and works: jar age, cookie expiry, a live check, the next step | read-only |
| `atlassian_login` | The exact `atlassian-cli login <service>` command to show the user | read-only |
| `jira_*` (63) | Every upstream Jira tool: issues, search, comments, transitions, sprints, boards, versions, links, worklogs, attachments, service desk, forms | 38 read-only, 25 write |
| `confluence_*` (35) | Every upstream Confluence tool: pages, search, comments, labels, attachments, history, templates, restrictions | 20 read-only, 15 write |

Every tool carries a title and all four annotation hints (read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world), so clients can auto-approve reads and confirm writes. The

readme.markdown:
# Memory.fit MCP

**Memory.fit** keeps your training, sleep, recovery and fuel in one place for the AI you already use. Your AI reads workouts from your watch and apps, sleep and HRV, and what you ate, then writes your week back: sessions, daily targets and meal plans, which show in the [Memory.fit app](https://memory.fit/app) on iPhone and Android.

This repository holds only the connection settings for Memory.fit MCP, a hosted server. There is nothing to run or build.

- **Address:** `https://api.memory.fit/mcp` (Streamable HTTP)
- **Sign-in:** OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration. Your AI opens the Memory.fit sign-in page; you choose what it may do. No key needed. AIs without sign-in can use a personal key from the app (Settings › AI agents › Use a key instead), sent as `Authorization: Bearer mem_pat_…`.
- **Needs:** a Memory.fit account, set up in the app first.

## Connect

| App | How |
|---|---|
| Claude | Settings › Connectors › Add custom connector, paste the address |
| ChatGPT | Settings › Apps and connectors › Create, paste the address |
| Grok, Grok Bot | Connectors › New connector › Custom, paste the address |
| Cursor | Install this plugin, or add `mcp.json` from this repo to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| Claude Code | `claude mcp add --transport http memory-fit https://api.memory.fit/mcp` |
| Codex | `codex mcp add memory-fit --url https://api.memory.fit/mcp` |
| Gemini CLI | `gemini extensions install https://github.com/Fun-Management-SRL/memory-fit-mcp` |
| Cline | MCP Servers › Remote Servers: name `memory-fit`, URL `https://api.memory.fit/mcp`, transport Streamable HTTP (or the JSON below) |
| Anything else | Any MCP client: the address above, then sign in |

Step-by-step pages for each AI: [memory.fit/ai-coaches](https://memory.fit/ai-coaches).

### Cline, or any client with a JSON settings file

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "memory-fit": {
      "type": "streamableHttp",
      "url": "https://api.memory.fit/mcp",
      "disabled": false
    }
  }
}
```

The first call opens the Memory.fit sign-in (OAuth 2.1). A client without OAuth can use a personal key from the app (Settings › AI agents › Use a key instead) as a header:

```json
"headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer mem_pat_..." }
```

## What your AI can do

- Read: workouts (Garmin, Wahoo, COROS, Polar, Suunto, Apple Health, Health Connect and more), sleep, HRV and resting heart rate, body composition, what you ate and drank, your races and goals.
- Write, with your permission: training sessions (sent to your watch), daily targets, meal plans, logged meals, notes for your other AIs.
- Check in: `get_updates` returns only what arrived since it last looked.

Memory.fit recommends nothing itself: the plans are your AI's, the data is yours. It is not medical advice.

## Links

- Website: https://memory.fit
- Privacy: https://memory.fit/privacy
- Terms: https://memory.fit/terms
- Support: support@memory.fit

The connection settings in this repository are MIT licensed. Memory.fit, the server and the app are not.

readme.markdown:
# Playwright Workspaces

> ✅ **Playwright Workspaces is now Generally Available!**

[Playwright Workspaces](https://aka.ms/pww/docs) is a fully managed service for end-to-end web testing, built on top of [Playwright](https://playwright.dev). With Playwright Workspaces, you can significantly speed up test execution by running tests in parallel using managed cloud-based browers. The service takes care of the underlying infrastructure and complexity, allowing you to validate your web app across major browsers on both Linux and Windows—so you can ship features faster and with greater confidence.

👉 [Get started with the Quickstart](https://aka.ms/pww/docs/quickstart)

## Documentation

The full documentation is now available on [**learn.microsoft.com**](https://aka.ms/pww/docs)

There you’ll learn how to:

- Run and scale Playwright tests in the cloud
- Optimize test suite performance and reliability
- Test across multiple browsers and operating systems
- Set up secure, region-aware test environments
- Integrate with CI/CD

## Playwright Cloud Browsers remote MCP (preview)

The [Playwright Cloud Browsers remote MCP server](https://aka.ms/pww/mcp/docs)
gives AI agents managed cloud browsers over Streamable HTTP. Agents can create a
browser session, navigate and inspect pages, interact with elements, and close
the session without installing Playwright or a browser locally.

The remote MCP server is in **preview**, separately from the generally available
Playwright Workspaces service. Preview features do not have a service-level
agreement and are not recommended for production workloads.

### Prerequisites and authentication

You need an Azure subscription, a Playwright workspace with access to the remote
MCP preview, its region and workspace ID, and an identity with permission to use
browser sessions in that workspace.

Use the endpoint for your workspace's region:

```text
https://<region>.mcp.playwright.microsoft.com/playwrightworkspaces/<workspace-id>/mcp
```

Replace both placeholders with your workspace values. Use Microsoft Entra ID
with a client that supports OAuth discovery. The server publishes
protected-resource metadata; your signed-in identity must also have the required
workspace RBAC access. See the [authentication and setup guide](https://aka.ms/pww/mcp/docs)
for permissions and supported compatibility options. Never commit access tokens
or paste them into prompts.

### Connect from VS Code or the GitHub Copilot app

- **VS Code:** Run **MCP: Add Server** from the Command Palette, select **HTTP**,
  enter the resolved workspace endpoint, and choose a configuration destination.
  Follow the server trust and Microsoft Entra sign-in prompts. See
  [Add MCP servers in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers).
- **GitHub Copilot app:** Open **Customize > MCP**, add a custom server using the
  resolved workspace endpoint, and follow the supported authentication prompts.
  See [Configuring MCP servers](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-copilot-app/customize-github-copilot-app#configuring-mcp-servers).

With the server connected, ask the agent to create a browser session, open
`https://example.com`, report the page's main heading, and close the session,
including on failure. Inspect the actual MCP tool calls and outputs to verify
the connection. See the [service guide](https://aka.ms/pww/mcp/docs) for session
limits, supported tools, and troubleshooting authentication, timeouts, and
expired sessions. Report service issues through this repository's
[issue tracker](https://github.com/Azure/playwright-workspaces/issues).

### Registry metadata

The server is published as `com.microsoft/playwright-cloud-browsers` in the
[Official MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0.1/servers/com.microsoft%2Fplaywright-cloud-browsers/versions/latest).
The root [`server.json`](./server.json) is a public copy of the published
metadata. Publication and metadata updates are managed by the service team;
changing this copy does not publish an update or establish a listing in
downstream client catalogs.

## Samples

Explore sample projects for different test runners:

- [Playwright Test with JavaScript/TypeScript](./samples/playwright-tests/)
- [NUnit with C#](./samples/.NET)
- [Python](./samples/playwright-python/)
- [Playwright Library projects](./samples/playwright-lib/)
- [Foundry Prompt Agents using Playwright Workspaces Remote MCP](./samples/remote-mcp/foundry-prompt-agents/)
- [Foundry Hosted Agents using Playwright Workspaces Remote MCP](./samples/remote-mcp/foundry-hosted-agents/)
- [App Verification Skills (verify skill)](./samples/app-verification-skills/)

## Migrating from Microsoft Playwright Testing

- See the [Migration Guide](./migration-guide.md) and [Troubleshooting Tips](./migration-troubleshooting.md)

## Issues

To report a bug, request a feature, or ask for a quote limit increase, please use the [Issues](https://github.com/Azure/playwright-workspaces/issues) section of this repository.

## More Resources

- [Documentation](https://aka.ms/pww/)

readme.markdown:
# Echo Memory

**Shared memory for AI agents, as a graph in your own database.** What Claude Code learns,
Cursor and Codex can recall. Every fact records who wrote it and when, and the server
never calls a model to store one.

<sub>Every line above is real output, captured from these commands against a throwaway
database. The transcript is at
[`.github/branding/demo-transcript.txt`](.github/branding/demo-transcript.txt).</sub>

> Your agents start every session from zero. The usual fix is a notes file you paste into
> context, which grows until it is mostly irrelevant to whatever you are asking. Echo
> Memory is the other shape: facts connected to each other, and a query that returns the
> few that matter. On the author's own 325 fact store that is **96.7% less context** for
> the same answer, with the answer still present 87.2% of the time across 1,190 queries
> the harness derived from their own answers.

```
write_episode                          query_memory
  billing ──uses──▸ Razorpay             "how do we take payments"
    │ written by claude-code               ▸ billing uses Razorpay, not Stripe
    │ supersedes ──▸ Stripe                  written by claude-code, 3 days ago
    └ no model invoked                     ▸ 1,372 tokens, not 41,838
```

## Install

**Requires:** Python 3.11+ and Docker (for the database).

```bash
pipx install echo-mem
echo-memory quickstart
```

`quickstart` starts the database, applies the schema, and prints the `claude mcp add`
line that registers it, filled in with the port it actually used. The Postgres image is
published, so nothing compiles.

Or use the hosted service and run no database at all:

```bash
pipx install echo-mem
echo-memory connect <key>          # a key from https://app.echo-mem.com
```

Then once per machine, so an agent knows *when* to record and recall rather than only
that the tools exist:

```bash
echo-memory install --global
```

> **Restart your client afterwards.** An MCP server is a long lived process that holds
> the code and config it started with, and an editable install does not change that.

> **The PyPI name is `echo-mem`, not `echo-memory`.** That name belongs to an unrelated
> hosted product. The import package and the CLI are both `echo_memory` / `echo-memory`;
> only the distribution name differs.

## Upgrading

```bash
pipx upgrade echo-mem
echo-memory init-db                # apply any new migrations
echo-memory reindex                # rebuild what the new code derives
```

Both steps, in that order, and neither is optional on a store that predates the version
you just installed.

**Skipping `init-db` fails loudly.** A read against a schema older than the code raises an
undefined column, which is the good case: it stops rather than answering from something it
half understands.

**Skipping `reindex` fails silently, which is worse.** Derived data that the new code reads
differently is still the old data, and nothing errors. Concretely, on an upgrade to 0.5.3
the lexical corpus statistics are treated as stale until rebuilt, so BM25 stays off and
your queries keep ranking by `ts_rank` while the setting reports as on. `reindex` rebuilds
the embeddings and those statistics together. `echo-memory health` tells you afterwards.

## Usage

```bash
echo-memory status                 # what each scope holds, and which agents have written
echo-memory health                 # a score, what is weak, and what to do about it
echo-memory dashboard --serve      # the graph, in a browser, localhost only

echo-memory why <fact_id>          # the full audit trail for one fact
echo-memory recall "<question>"    # query the store from a terminal
echo-memory export                 # everything, as JSON

echo-memory install --for cursor   # wire one client, project scoped
echo-memory adopt                  # wire every MCP client on the machine, each with its own id

echo-memory infer-causal-hints     # type the facts whose own sentence states a cause (dry run)

echo-memory eval                   # retrieval quality against your own store
echo-memory eval --context         # what a recall costs against injecting everything
echo-memory eval --context --sweep # the same, as a curve across corpus size
echo-memory eval-external locomo <path>       # LoCoMo, the corpus the published figures use
echo-memory eval-external longmemeval <path>  # LongMemEval, the same
echo-memory calibrate              # is entity resolution trustworthy on your data
echo-memory benchmark              # write, query and digest latency
```

### The seven MCP tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `write_episode` | Store entities and the facts connecting them. No model call. |
| `query_memory` | Hybrid vector and full text retrieval, fused by reciprocal rank. Full text ranks by BM25. Takes `as_of` to read the store as it stood at an instant, and `about` to return the facts recorded against one or two named entities. |
| `trace_cause` | Causal chains through the entities a subject matches, not a ranked list. |
| `record_recall_save` | Mark that a recalled fact saved re explaining something. Refuses a fact no read returned. |
| `get_audit_log` | Every change to memory, with a plain language reason. |
| `pending_documents` | Memory files this project wrote that the graph has not heard about. |
| `mark_ingested` | Close one of those out. |

## What you get

**A graph, not a list.** Entities are nodes and a fact is an edge between two of them.
Two sessions that never knew about each other resolve onto the same entity by name, so
the second inherits what the first learned.

**Bounded retrieval, designed but not built.** The plan is that old, rarely read memory
demotes into higher level summaries over time, with nothing discarded and every summary
still edged back to the facts it came from. None of it exists yet: there is no tiering,
no summarisation, and retrieval today walks every active fact in the scope. It is
described in [`docs/designs/`](docs/designs/) and l

…

readme.markdown:
# Apiary Memory MCP

> **Also known as:** Apiary Memory · 记忆蜂巢 · Memory Hive · 蜂巢 ·
> `apiary-memory` on PyPI and `io.github.330899935/apiary-memory` on the MCP Registry (from v0.2.0) ·
> old names `memory-hive-mcp` / `hive-memory` (v0.1.9 and earlier) still install and still work.
> Not affiliated with [hive.com](https://hive.com) (team collaboration) or the `hive-mcp` Claude Code plugin.

**Local-first personal memory for AI agents, over MCP.** Your agents can search what you have
confirmed and propose what they think you should keep; **only you can confirm it.** Everything
lives in one file on your own disk, and nothing is sent anywhere.

It runs on its own. A working SQLite memory store ships inside this package — no account, no
cloud, no daemon, no dependencies.

```bash
pip install apiary-memory
```

**Desktop app, no terminal:** download [`apiary-memory-0.2.0.mcpb`](https://github.com/330899935/apiary-memory/releases/download/v0.2.0/apiary-memory-0.2.0.mcpb) and double-click it.

Measured on 2026-10-27, on one MacBook with the Hive running locally — script and raw output in [`bench/`](bench/):

| Measure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Search latency | **p95 111 ms**, p50 76 ms (warm, includes HTTP) |
| Retrieval | correct entry in **top-5 for 97.5%** of 40 trials |
| Corpus | **1,303 entries · 2.39 M chars · 45 days**, plaintext only |

*Retrieval used each entry's own title as the query — an easy set. It shows the index is complete and ranks correctly on exact terms, not how well it answers a question asked in your own words. Run [`bench/bench_search.py`](bench/bench_search.py) on your own Hive.*

---

## What you get without the app

A complete, if modest, memory server. On a machine with nothing else installed:

| Call | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `initialize` | answered locally, protocol `2024-11-05` |
| `tools/list` | answered locally, six tools |
| `propose` | **writes to a real database** on your disk |
| `recall` | **searches that database** and returns ranked entries |
| `get_context` | a digest of what you confirmed most recently |
| `manage` | read one entry, list what is pending, forget, restore |
| `say` / `board` | a shared message board for coordinating several agents |

Storage is SQLite at `~/.memory-hive/hive.db` by default. Search is lexical — character bigrams
for Chinese, words for Latin script — so it ranks well when the words overlap and finds nothing
when they do not. There are no embeddings and no vector index. Every response says
`"mode": "local"` so you can always tell which engine answered.

**Without the app, the database is plain SQLite: it is not encrypted.** That is stated here
rather than discovered later — see [Honest limits](#honest-limits).

## What the app adds

[Apiary Memory for macOS](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6806992983) is the same design with the
expensive parts built: eight vaults with four of them locked behind a PIN (Argon2id-wrapped key,
AES-256 at rest), a daily evolution log, multi-agent identity management, and a UI for reading
and confirming. It also answers MCP itself, with richer ranking.

If the app is running, this package uses it and leaves the local file alone. If it is not, the
local store answers. You do not have to choose up front:

| `HIVE_MODE` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `auto` (default) | Ask the app. Use the local store **only if the app is unreachable.** |
| `local` | Never touch the network. Always use the local store. |
| `remote` | Only the app. A connection failure is an error, not a reroute. |

One rule holds in every mode: **if the app is running and answers with an error, that error is
returned unchanged.** Falling back on a refusal would write your memory into a second database
while your client believed it had reached the app. Silent data forking is worse than an error
message, so a reply from the app is final. The fallback fires on a connection failure, and on
nothing else.

## Measured on the app

The numbers below come from the macOS app's local HTTP service on one MacBook — **not** from
this package's SQLite store, which is a different engine over a different dataset. Mixing the
two would be the usual benchmark trick, so they are kept apart.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Store size (four plaintext vaults) | **1,356 entries**, 2.52M chars, 47 distinct days |
| Retrieval hit rate | Top-5 **92.5%**, Top-20 **95.0%** (n=40) |
| Latency (local HTTP, incl. round trip) | p50 **90 ms**, p95 **127 ms** |

Measured 2026-10-29 against the live service. The hit-rate queries were each entry's own
title — the easy case. It shows the index is complete; it does not show that free-form
questions land. A separate pilot using plainly-phrased questions found the right entry in the
top 5 only twice out of roughly a dozen, which is the biggest known weakness of this version.

The four encrypted vaults are excluded from the count because they are unreadable by design.
A load test at 1,000,000 synthetic entries gave 0.6 s warm search, 5.3 GB RSS and a 1.0 GB
index — see [`bench/`](https://github.com/330899935/apiary-memory/tree/main/bench) for the
script and raw output.

## Install

```bash
pip install apiary-memory        # the server: apiary-memory (was memory-hive-mcp)
                                 # the human's CLI: apiary-memory-cli (was memory-hive-mcp-cli)
```

Python 3.8 or newer. There is nothing else to install — the package uses only the standard
library, and `sqlite3` is part of it.

From a checkout:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/330899935/apiary-memory
cd apiary-memory
PYTHONPATH=src python -m hive_mcp.stdio
```

## Connect a client

Any MCP host that can run a stdio command will work. The minimum is the command; everything else
is optional.

**Claude Desktop** — `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "apiary-memory": {
      "command": "apiary-memory",
      "env": { "HIVE_MODE": "local" }
    }
  }
}
```

**Cursor** — `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, sam

…

tools.description: read

tools.name: propose
tools.description: write

tools.name: manage
tools.description: read/write

tools.name: get_context

# FINSEC — Certified SEC Memory MCP Server

[![Zero Hallucination](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hallucination_Rate-0.00%25_(∂²=0)-purple.svg)](https://finsec.caleralabs.com)

Official **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** connector for **Calera Labs FINSEC**. Connects AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Zed, VS Code, and custom autonomous swarms) directly to **4.06M certified SEC EDGAR facts** powered by the **Calera Episteme-1 Engine**.

> **"Frontier Models Reason — The Calera Lattice Supplies Ground Truth."**

---

## ⚡ Key Guarantees

* **0.00% Statistical Hallucination:** Fact recall is deterministic and geometric ($A_4$ Pentatope lattice memory). No language model exists in the fact retrieval path.
* **2026-07-28 Stateless Protocol Core:** Fully compliant with the 2026-07-28 Stateless MCP Specification (SEP-2243, SEP-2575, SEP-2549) with sub-5ms zero-handshake direct tool calls and intelligent caching (`ttlMs: 86400000`).
* **Cryptographic Provenance:** Every returned financial metric includes exact SEC filing accessions, dates, concepts, and SHA-256 audit hashes.
* **Honest Refusal (`SAFE_REFUSAL`):** If a metric is not present in official SEC filings or is ambiguous, the engine returns an honest safe refusal rather than confabulating numbers.
* **Ultra-Low Latency & High Gross Margins:** Sub-25ms response serialization with low token footprint mode.

---

## 🚀 1-Click Quickstart Integrations

### 1. Cursor IDE

Add the following to your project's `.cursor/mcp.json` (or global Cursor Settings → Features → MCP):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "finsec": {
      "url": "https://finsec.caleralabs.com/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "X-License-Key": "clabs_live_YOUR_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```
*(Get your free API key at [dashboard.caleralabs.com](https://dashboard.caleralabs.com))*

---

### 2. Claude Desktop

Add to your `claude_desktop_config.json`:
* **macOS:** `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
* **Windows:** `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`
* **Linux:** `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "finsec": {
      "url": "https://finsec.caleralabs.com/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "X-License-Key": "clabs_live_YOUR_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

---

### 3. Smithery CLI (1-Click Terminal Command)

Install automatically across Claude or Cursor using Smithery ([smithery.ai/servers/calera-labs/finsec](https://smithery.ai/servers/calera-labs/finsec)):

```bash
# For Claude Desktop
npx -y @smithery/cli install financesec-mcp --client claude

# For Cursor
npx -y @smithery/cli install financesec-mcp --client cursor
```

---

### 4. Zed Editor

Add to `~/.config/zed/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "experimental.context_servers": {
    "finsec": {
      "command": {
        "url": "https://finsec.caleralabs.com/mcp",
        "headers": {
          "X-License-Key": "clabs_live_YOUR_KEY"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

---

### 5. Stdio JSON-RPC & Zero-Config Auto-Bridge

For local agent workflows (Cursor, Claude Code, Antigravity, or custom runners) using stdio:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "finsec": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@caleralabs/finsec-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

#### 🔗 Zero-Config Cross-MCP Credential Sharing
When executed via stdio, `@caleralabs/finsec-mcp` automatically discovers and links credentials stored at `~/.calera/icx.env` or created when running `@caleralabs/llm-vm-mcp` (`claim_free_icx_tokens`). 

A single Calera API key (`ICX_API_KEY`) unifies your entire AI stack:
* **FINSEC Ground Truth:** 4.06M certified SEC EDGAR facts with zero hallucination.
* **LLM-VM Execution:** Hermetic zero-escape MicroVM sandboxes.

Once connected, simply ask your agent in plain English:

# Apiary Memory MCP

> **Also known as:** Apiary Memory · 记忆蜂巢 · Memory Hive · 蜂巢 ·
> `apiary-memory` on PyPI and `io.github.330899935/apiary-memory` on the MCP Registry (from v0.2.0) ·
> old names `memory-hive-mcp` / `hive-memory` (v0.1.9 and earlier) still install and still work.
> Not affiliated with [hive.com](https://hive.com) (team collaboration) or the `hive-mcp` Claude Code plugin.

**Local-first personal memory for AI agents, over MCP.** Your agents can search what you have
confirmed and propose what they think you should keep; **only you can confirm it.** Everything
lives in one file on your own disk, and nothing is sent anywhere.

It runs on its own. A working SQLite memory store ships inside this package — no account, no
cloud, no daemon, no dependencies.

```bash
pip install apiary-memory
```

**Desktop app, no terminal:** download [`apiary-memory-0.2.0.mcpb`](https://github.com/330899935/apiary-memory/releases/download/v0.2.0/apiary-memory-0.2.0.mcpb) and double-click it.

Measured on 2026-10-27, on one MacBook with the Hive running locally — script and raw output in [`bench/`](bench/):

| Measure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Search latency | **p95 111 ms**, p50 76 ms (warm, includes HTTP) |
| Retrieval | correct entry in **top-5 for 97.5%** of 40 trials |
| Corpus | **1,303 entries · 2.39 M chars · 45 days**, plaintext only |

*Retrieval used each entry's own title as the query — an easy set. It shows the index is complete and ranks correctly on exact terms, not how well it answers a question asked in your own words. Run [`bench/bench_search.py`](bench/bench_search.py) on your own Hive.*

---

## What you get without the app

A complete, if modest, memory server. On a machine with nothing else installed:

| Call | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `initialize` | answered locally, protocol `2024-11-05` |
| `tools/list` | answered locally, six tools |
| `propose` | **writes to a real database** on your disk |
| `recall` | **searches that database** and returns ranked entries |
| `get_context` | a digest of what you confirmed most recently |
| `manage` | read one entry, list what is pending, forget, restore |
| `say` / `board` | a shared message board for coordinating several agents |

Storage is SQLite at `~/.memory-hive/hive.db` by default. Search is lexical — character bigrams
for Chinese, words for Latin script — so it ranks well when the words overlap and finds nothing
when they do not. There are no embeddings and no vector index. Every response says
`"mode": "local"` so you can always tell which engine answered.

**Without the app, the database is plain SQLite: it is not encrypted.** That is stated here
rather than discovered later — see [Honest limits](#honest-limits).

## What the app adds

[Apiary Memory for macOS](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6806992983) is the same design with the
expensive parts built: eight vaults with four of them locked behind a PIN (Argon2id-wrapped key,
AES-256 at rest), a daily evolution log, multi-agent identity management, and a UI for reading
and confirming. It also answers MCP itself, with richer ranking.

If the app is running, this package uses it and leaves the local file alone. If it is not, the
local store answers. You do not have to choose up front:

| `HIVE_MODE` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `auto` (default) | Ask the app. Use the local store **only if the app is unreachable.** |
| `local` | Never touch the network. Always use the local store. |
| `remote` | Only the app. A connection failure is an error, not a reroute. |

One rule holds in every mode: **if the app is running and answers with an error, that error is
returned unchanged.** Falling back on a refusal would write your memory into a second database
while your client believed it had reached the app. Silent data forking is worse than an error
message, so a reply from the app is final. The fallback fires on a connection failure, and on
nothing else.

## Measured on the app

The numbers below come from the macOS app's local HTTP service on one MacBook — **not** from
this package's SQLite store, which is a different engine over a different dataset. Mixing the
two would be the usual benchmark trick, so they are kept apart.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Store size (four plaintext vaults) | **1,356 entries**, 2.52M chars, 47 distinct days |
| Retrieval hit rate | Top-5 **92.5%**, Top-20 **95.0%** (n=40) |
| Latency (local HTTP, incl. round trip) | p50 **90 ms**, p95 **127 ms** |

Measured 2026-10-29 against the live service. The hit-rate queries were each entry's own
title — the easy case. It shows the index is complete; it does not show that free-form
questions land. A separate pilot using plainly-phrased questions found the right entry in the
top 5 only twice out of roughly a dozen, which is the biggest known weakness of this version.

The four encrypted vaults are excluded from the count because they are unreadable by design.
A load test at 1,000,000 synthetic entries gave 0.6 s warm search, 5.3 GB RSS and a 1.0 GB
index — see [`bench/`](https://github.com/330899935/apiary-memory/tree/main/bench) for the
script and raw output.

## Install

```bash
pip install apiary-memory        # the server: apiary-memory (was memory-hive-mcp)
                                 # the human's CLI: apiary-memory-cli (was memory-hive-mcp-cli)
```

Python 3.8 or newer. There is nothing else to install — the package uses only the standard
library, and `sqlite3` is part of it.

From a checkout:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/330899935/apiary-memory
cd apiary-memory
PYTHONPATH=src python -m hive_mcp.stdio
```

## Connect a client

Any MCP host that can run a stdio command will work. The minimum is the command; everything else
is optional.

**Claude Desktop** — `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "apiary-memory": {
      "command": "apiary-memory",
      "env": { "HIVE_MODE": "local" }
    }
  }
}
```

**Cursor** — `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, sam

# Atlaso — remote MCP server

**Atlaso is an AI memory layer: one shared, persistent memory across every AI tool you connect.**

Tell it once in one tool, and it's already there in the next. Atlaso recalls the
context that matters before each turn and captures the durable facts after — your
decisions, your preferences, and where you left off.

This repository documents Atlaso's **hosted MCP server**. Atlaso is a managed
service, so there is nothing to self-host and no server code here — you connect
to the endpoint below and authorize in your browser.

- **Endpoint:** `https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp`
- **Transport:** Streamable HTTP
- **Auth:** OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration — your MCP client walks you
  through it; there are no API keys to paste
- **Website:** https://www.atlaso.ai
- **Docs:** https://docs.atlaso.ai

## Why this exists
Claude Desktop, Zed, Cline and other MCP clients have no memory of their own that reaches your coding tools. This hosted server gives any MCP client the same memory your coding tools share: decisions made in long chats, research and notes, preferences that should follow you. Memory works when the model calls the tools (remember, recall, forget); a skill can make that routine. Add `https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp` as a connector and sign in. [Claude Desktop](https://www.atlaso.ai/for/claude-desktop) · [Any MCP tool](https://docs.atlaso.ai/tools/custom-mcp)

## Connect

Any MCP client that supports remote servers can connect. Add
`https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp` as a connector and authorize in the browser when
prompted.

**Claude Desktop / claude.ai** — Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector →
paste the endpoint → Connect → authorize.

**Cursor, VS Code, and other MCP clients** — add it as a remote MCP server:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "atlaso": {
      "url": "https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

**Terminal-based tools** (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity) get a richer
integration than MCP alone — automatic recall before each turn and automatic
capture after, via hooks. One command sets all of them up:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://atlaso.ai/install.sh | bash    # macOS / Linux
irm https://atlaso.ai/install.ps1 | iex           # Windows
```

That installs the `atlaso` CLI, links the machine (creating your account if you
don't have one), then asks which of your AI tools should share the memory.

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `recall(query, limit=5)` | Search your memory for notes relevant to `query`. Returns a ranked list of `{id, content}`. Read-only. |
| `remember(text, polarity)` | Save a durable note — a decision, preference, or gotcha. `polarity` is one of `positive`, `open`, `cautionary`, `negative`. Returns the new id. |
| `recent(limit=10)` | List the most recent memories, newest first. Read-only. |
| `forget(id)` | Permanently delete a memory by id. Destructive and not undoable. |
| `status()` | Connection state, how many memories are stored and pending, and your memory health score. Read-only. |

Every recall carries a verdict on whether a memory is settled or contested, so
the model isn't acting on shaky context.

## Memory scopes

Memories are either **personal** (they follow you everywhere) or **project**
(scoped to the repository or workspace you were in). Both are recalled
automatically in the right place — you don't manage scopes by hand.

## Privacy

Secrets are scrubbed before anything is stored. Data is encrypted in transit and
at rest. Your memory is never used to train AI models and never sold. On the free
plan it is never sent to any LLM at all. You can delete any single memory, or your
whole account, at any time.

## Pricing

Free for one device and one tool. Pro is **$10/month** for unlimited devices and
tools sharing one memory, plus Ambient Memory, background enrichment, Ask your
memory, and JSON export. Build is **$25/month** and adds a developer memory API.

## Registry

Listed in the official MCP Registry as `io.github.imashishkh21/atlaso`. The
[`server.json`](./server.json) in this repository is the published manifest.

---

Atlaso is a product of Atlaso Labs Inc. This repository is documentation for the
hosted service; the service itself is not open source.

# mcps

**MCP servers that let an AI assistant do a company's everyday work.** Most are
for services people use anywhere, such as Google Workspace, Notion, Bitwarden,
Porkbun, Expo, the app stores and European banks; a second line is for
companies in Romania, to file with ANAF, follow the trade register, invoice
through Oblio and read the National Bank's rates.

Each server connects an MCP client, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, VS Code
or Cursor, to one service. They are built on one toolkit, so every tool says
what it can change: `read` (it changes nothing), `write` (it changes something
in your account) or `money` (it moves money, makes or unmakes a legal or fiscal
document, or commits you in a comparable way, such as a bank consent). Your
client asks you before each `money` call.

[foreverworks.github.io/mcps](https://foreverworks.github.io/mcps/) presents the servers by who they are for, each with its documentation.

Under each server's name: how settled it is, then how many tools it has and the most they can do. **Stable**: in daily use, and its tools keep their shape. **Beta**: works and is in use, but is new, still growing, or reads web pages its service may change. **Experimental**: rests on something that can break without notice, or covers only part of the service.

## For companies in Romania

The paperwork a company in Romania, and the people who run it, do online: e-invoices and declarations with ANAF, filings at the trade register, invoicing, and the National Bank's exchange rates. Each README ends with the other servers we found for that service, and what this one adds.

| Server | What it does |
|---|---|
| [ ANAF e-Factura](servers/anaf-efactura)<sub>Stable20 tools, including **money**</sub> | Read, check and file a Romanian company's e-invoices and e-Transport declarations with ANAF. |
| [ ANAF SPV](servers/anaf-spv)<sub>Beta16 tools, including **money**</sub> | Download what ANAF posts to your SPV inbox, request documents, and validate or file declarations. |
| [ BNR exchange rates](servers/bnr)<sub>Stable5 tools, read-only</sub> | Look up the National Bank of Romania's rate for any day, and convert amounts to and from RON. |
| [ Oblio](servers/oblio)<sub>Stable17 tools, including **money**</sub> | Issue and track a Romanian company's invoices on Oblio, with totals computed as ANAF checks them. |
| [ ONRC trade register](servers/onrc)<sub>Beta9 tools, read and write</sub> | Follow your filings at Romania's trade register, with their documents, fee notes and invoices. |

## For everyone

Servers for services people use anywhere. We built each one because the servers we found did less, or there were none; each README's last section names them and says what this one adds.

| Server | What it does |
|---|---|
| [ App Store and Google Play](servers/app-stores)<sub>Beta7 tools, read and write</sub> | Read and answer App Store and Google Play reviews, and see TestFlight feedback and crash logs. |
| [ Bitwarden](servers/bitwarden)<sub>Stable12 tools, read and write</sub> | Give your assistant its own Bitwarden vault to create logins, type passwords and read 2FA codes. |
| [ Expo Application Services](servers/eas)<sub>Beta23 tools, including **money**</sub> | Find out why an Expo build, workflow run or store submission failed, and roll out updates. |
| [ Enable Banking](servers/enable-banking)<sub>Stable10 tools, including **money**</sub> | Read, search and export statements and balances from banks across Europe, without moving money. |
| [ Google Workspace](servers/google)<sub>Stable115 tools, read and write</sub> | Search and work in Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets and Slides across several Google accounts. |
| [ Home Assistant](servers/home-assistant)<sub>Beta10 tools, read and write</sub> | Read your Home Assistant's states, areas and history, and run its actions, approving locks first. |
| [ Notion](servers/notion)<sub>Stable27 tools, read and write</sub> | Search, read and write your Notion workspaces, with pages as Markdown and typed database queries. |
| [ Porkbun](servers/porkbun)<sub>Beta113 tools, including **money**</sub> | Register domains and manage DNS, hosting and mail at Porkbun, with every purchase confirmed first. |
| [ Trademark search](servers/trademarks)<sub>Beta6 tools, read-only</sub> | Check whether a name is already a registered or pending trademark in the US or the EU. |
| [ TypeSafe](servers/typesafe)<sub>Beta3 tools, read-only</sub> | Get calibrated yes or no answers, choices and scores from TypeSafe's Jev, for one item or 1000 rows. |

## Extras

These work, and we use them, but each is built for one particular setup or on an app's unofficial API, so they are not published to npm, the MCP Registry or as desktop bundles. Run them from a clone, and read the README first: it says what the server depends on and what can break.

| Server | What it does |
|---|---|
| [ Bolt Food receipts](servers/bolt-food)<sub>Experimental8 tools, read-only</sub> | Read your Bolt Food orders as itemised receipts matched to card charges, through an unofficial API. |
| [ Device broker](servers/devices)<sub>Experimental10 tools, read and write</sub> | Share your own Android emulators, iOS simulators and desktops between AI agents, in fair turns. |
| [ Glovo receipts](servers/glovo)<sub>Experimental8 tools, read-only</sub> | Read your Glovo orders as itemised receipts matched to card charges, through an unofficial API. |
| [ Printer and scanner](servers/printer)<sub>Experimental10 tools, read and write</sub> | Print, scan and check paper and toner on a network printer, with greys corrected for that printer. |
| [ Local RAG](servers/rag)<sub>Beta10 tools, read and write</sub> | Index your PDFs, scans and documents locally, and search them with hybrid retrieval and a reranker. |
| [ Smart home](servers/smart-home)<sub>Experimental7 tools, read and write</sub> | Press the buttons of a TV, heater or fan remote by name through a BroadLink IR blaster. |

# agent-in-browser

**A real browser for any AI agent, any model, and any test runner** — one dependency-free binary.

<sub>Real recording, not a mock-up. The agent reads the page as a snapshot with element refs, types, fills the form and clicks, first in Chrome (CDP), then in Firefox (WebDriver BiDi). Regenerate it with `task demo`.</sub>

`agent-in-browser` is an open take on "Claude in Chrome". It doesn't need an extension or a vendor-specific runtime. It drives the browsers you already have through their native automation protocols:

| Browser | Protocol | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome, Chrome Beta/Canary, Chromium, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, Opera | Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) | ✅ |
| Firefox, Firefox Developer Edition / Nightly | WebDriver BiDi | ✅ |
| Safari | WebDriver (safaridriver) | 🛣 detected, [roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) |

It's available three ways, all backed by the same tool catalogue:

1. **MCP server** (`agent-in-browser mcp`): plugs into Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, VS Code/Copilot, Zed, opencode and any other MCP client, whatever model sits behind it.
2. **Shell CLI** (`agent-in-browser call <tool> …`): for agents without MCP, for scripts, and for humans. Calls share one persistent browser.
3. **Scenario runner** (`agent-in-browser run test.yaml --browser chrome,firefox`): replays tool calls as automated tests across a browser matrix, with JUnit/JSON reports.

An **agent skill** ([`skills/agent-in-browser/SKILL.md`](skills/agent-in-browser/SKILL.md)) ships inside the binary and teaches agents the workflow.

## Install

```bash
# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Gwakko/agent-in-browser/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Gwakko/agent-in-browser/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

# Homebrew (macOS / Linux)
brew install gwakko/tap/agent-in-browser

# With Go
go install github.com/gwakko/agent-in-browser/cmd/agent-in-browser@latest

# From a checkout (needs Task: https://taskfile.dev)
task install            # → ~/.local/bin/agent-in-browser + alias `aib`
```

## Connect your agent

```bash
agent-in-browser setup claude-code --write    # runs `claude mcp add --scope user …`
agent-in-browser setup cursor --write         # merges ~/.cursor/mcp.json (a .bak is kept)
agent-in-browser setup codex --write          # appends to ~/.codex/config.toml
agent-in-browser setup gemini --write         # ~/.gemini/settings.json
agent-in-browser setup vscode                 # prints the snippet for .vscode/mcp.json
agent-in-browser skill install --for claude   # ~/.claude/skills/agent-in-browser (also: codex, agents, --dir)
```

**Claude Desktop, one click:** download `agent-in-browser-<version>.mcpb` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Gwakko/agent-in-browser/releases/latest) and open it. It also appears in the [MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/) as `io.github.Gwakko/agent-in-browser`.

Without `--write`, `setup` only prints the config. Pass browser options through with `--args "--browser firefox --headless"`. See [docs/integrations.md](docs/integrations.md) for every client.

## Use it from the shell

```bash
agent-in-browser call navigate url=localhost:3000
agent-in-browser call snapshot
#   - textbox "Email" [ref=e3] (required, type=email)
#   - button "Sign up" [ref=e7]
agent-in-browser call type ref=e3 text=me@example.com
agent-in-browser call click ref=e7
agent-in-browser call wait_for text=Welcome
agent-in-browser call console_messages level=error
agent-in-browser call screenshot            # → prints PNG path
agent-in-browser stop
```

Useful flags (they work anywhere on the command line): `--browser firefox`, `--headless`, `--instance work` for a second, independent browser, `--endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9222` to attach to a browser you started yourself, and `--viewport 390x844`.

## Test scenarios

```yaml
name: signup
browsers: [chrome, firefox]
steps:
  - navigate: http://localhost:3000/signup
  - fill_form:
      fields:
        - { selector: "#email", value: "qa@example.com" }
        - { match: "I accept the terms", value: true }
  - click: Sign up
  - wait_for: { text: "Welcome" }
  - assert: { url_contains: "/dashboard", no_console_errors: true }
```

```bash
agent-in-browser run tests/*.yaml --browser chrome,firefox,edge --junit report.xml
```

Full format: [skills/agent-in-browser/references/scenarios.md](skills/agent-in-browser/references/scenarios.md).

## Tools

`browser_status` · `browsers_installed` · `tabs_list` · `tab_new` · `tab_select` · `tab_close` · `navigate` · `snapshot` · `find` · `click` · `hover` · `type` · `press_key` · `fill_form` · `scroll` · `wait_for` · `get_text` · `screenshot` · `evaluate` · `console_messages` · `network_requests` · `resize` · `browser_close`

Arguments are documented in [docs/tools.md](docs/tools.md), which `task docs:tools` generates.

## How it works

```
 agent ──MCP/stdio──┐
 shell ──call───────┼──▶ tools ──▶ session ──▶ Driver ──CDP──────▶ Chrome / Edge / Brave / …
 CI ────run yaml────┘     (one catalogue)  (attach|launch)  └─BiDi─────▶ Firefox
                                                            page lib (injected JS):
                                                            snapshot · refs · fill · find
```

- The browser runs on a **dedicated profile** (`~/.agent-in-browser/profiles/<instance>-<browser>`) and is **detached**, so it survives MCP server restarts. Separate CLI calls reuse it through `~/.agent-in-browser/instances/<name>.json`.
- Page understanding (snapshot, refs, form filling) is **injected JavaScript** that works the same in every engine. Trusted input, screenshots, tabs and console/network capture come from each protocol's driver.
- Details: [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) · browser notes: [docs/browsers.md](docs/browsers.md) · plans: [docs/roadmap.md](docs/roadmap.md).

## Development

```bash
task build      # bin/agent-in-browser
task te

readme.markdown:
# Murphy's Laws

A comprehensive collection of Murphy's Laws - humorous observations about life's tendency for things to go wrong.

Available on the **Web**, with iOS and Android releases forthcoming.

## Platforms

- **Web**: <https://murphys-laws.com> (PWA - installable, works offline)
- **iOS**: Coming Soon
- **Android**: Coming Soon

## AI & Developer Integration

Four official ways to integrate Murphy's Laws. No API key for reads.

| Package | npm | Purpose |
|---------|-----|---------|
| [`murphys-laws-sdk`](sdk/) | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/murphys-laws-sdk.svg?label=)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-sdk) | Typed TypeScript client, zero deps |
| [`murphys-laws-cli`](cli/) | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/murphys-laws-cli.svg?label=)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-cli) | Command-line interface (`npx murphys-laws-cli`) |
| [`murphys-laws-mcp`](mcp/) | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/murphys-laws-mcp.svg?label=)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-mcp) | Model Context Protocol server for AI agents |
| [REST API](shared/docs/API.md) | - | Public HTTP API at `https://murphys-laws.com/api/v1/` |

Full details and examples on the [developer landing page](https://murphys-laws.com/developers).

### REST API

Public API at `https://murphys-laws.com/api/v1/`, no auth required for reads.

- [API Documentation](shared/docs/API.md)
- [OpenAPI spec](https://murphys-laws.com/openapi.json)
- [llms.txt](https://murphys-laws.com/llms.txt) | [llms-full.txt](https://murphys-laws.com/llms-full.txt)

### TypeScript SDK

[`murphys-laws-sdk`](sdk/) on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-sdk) is a tiny typed client over the REST API with zero runtime dependencies.

```ts
import { MurphysLawsClient } from 'murphys-laws-sdk';
const law = await new MurphysLawsClient().getRandomLaw();
```

### Command-line interface

[`murphys-laws-cli`](cli/) on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-cli) wraps the API for scripts and terminal use.

```bash
npx murphys-laws-cli random
npx murphys-laws-cli search "computer" --limit 3
```

### MCP Server (Model Context Protocol)

An [MCP server](mcp/) lets AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code Copilot) query Murphy's Laws directly.

Quick start, no clone needed:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "murphys-laws": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "murphys-laws-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

7 tools: `search_laws`, `get_random_law`, `get_law_of_the_day`, `get_law`, `list_categories`, `get_laws_by_category`, `submit_law`.

See [mcp/README.md](mcp/README.md) or [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-mcp), or the [developer landing page](https://murphys-laws.com/developers) for the full picture.

## Repository Structure

This is a monorepo containing:

```
murphys-laws/
├── backend/        # Node.js API server (TypeScript runtime via tsx)
├── web/            # Web application (TypeScript + Vite)
├── mcp/            # MCP server for AI agent integration (npm: murphys-laws-mcp)
├── sdk/            # TypeScript SDK over the public REST API (npm: murphys-laws-sdk)
├── cli/            # Command-line interface (npm: murphys-laws-cli)
├── ios/            # iOS app (Swift + SwiftUI)
├── android/        # Android app (Kotlin + Jetpack Compose)
└── shared/         # Shared resources and documentation
```

## Quick Start

### Backend (API Server)

```bash
cd backend
npm install
npm run build:db # Build SQLite database
npm run dev # Start API server
npm start # Run API from src/server/api-server.ts via tsx
```

### Web Application

```bash
cd web
npm install
npm run dev # Start dev server
```

### iOS App

```bash
cd ios
open MurphysLaws.xcodeproj
# Press ⌘R to run
```

### Android App

```bash
cd android
./gradlew assembleDebug
# Or open in Android Studio
```

## Documentation

- **Architecture**: [Mobile Architecture Guide](shared/docs/MOBILE-ARCHITECTURE.md)
- **MCP Server**: [MCP README](mcp/README.md)
- **API**: [API Documentation](shared/docs/API.md)
- **iOS**: [iOS PRD](shared/docs/MOBILE-IOS-PRD.md)
- **Android**: [Android PRD](shared/docs/MOBILE-ANDROID-PRD.md)
- **Deployment**: [Deployment Guide](shared/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md)
- **Repository Structure**: [Repository Structure Guide](shared/docs/MOBILE-REPOSITORY-STRUCTURE.md)

## Testing

```bash
# Run all tests (backend, web, SDK, CLI, and MCP)
npm test

# Test a subset only
npm run test:backend   # Backend Vitest suite
npm run test:web       # Web Vitest suite only (no E2E)
npm run test:web:e2e   # Web E2E (Playwright) only
```

## Development

### Prerequisites

- Node.js 22+
- For iOS: macOS, Xcode 15+
- For Android: Android Studio Hedgehog+, JDK 17+

### Install Dependencies

```bash
# Install all dependencies (root and workspaces)
npm run install:all

# Or install individually
cd backend && npm install
cd web && npm install
```

### Run Development Servers

```bash
# Run backend + web concurrently
npm run dev

# Or run individually
npm run dev:backend
npm run dev:web
```

**Note**: The `predev` script automatically cleans up any orphaned processes using ports 8787 and 5175 before starting.

### Troubleshooting Port Issues

If you encounter `EADDRINUSE` errors (port already in use):

```bash
# Check which processes are using development ports
npm run cleanup-ports

# Automatically kill processes using development ports
npm run cleanup-ports -- --kill

# Or manually check and kill
lsof -i :8787  # Check API port
lsof -i :5175  # Check frontend port
kill <PID>     # Kill the process
```

## Building

```bash
# Generate OpenAPI and build the web app
npm run build

# Build specific platform

npm run build:backend:db

- Backend runs TypeScript source directly with `tsx` (no JS build step required for startup).
- Canonical backend runtime entrypoint: `backend/src/server/api-server.ts`.
- PM2 runtime uses Node loader: `node --import tsx`.

# sqlite-sidecar-mcp

**An agent-safe MCP sidecar for one live SQLite database.**

It gives an AI agent controlled access to a database that another application already owns,
and it limits the damage that an authorized but mistaken agent can cause.

[![ci][ci-shield]][ci-url]
[![license][license-shield]][license-url]
[![ghcr][ghcr-shield]][ghcr-url]
[![dotnet][dotnet-shield]][dotnet-url]

<details>
  <summary>Contents</summary>

- [About the project](#about-the-project)
- [Built with](#built-with)
- [Getting started](#getting-started)
- [The eight tools](#the-eight-tools)
- [Permissions](#permissions)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Deployment](#deployment)
- [Security](#security)
- [Contributing](#contributing)
- [License](#license)
- [Contact](#contact)
- [Acknowledgments](#acknowledgments)

</details>

## About the project

An application owns a SQLite file. You want an agent to read it, and perhaps to change a few rows.
Handing the agent a SQL connection gives it the whole file and one `DELETE` with a wrong predicate
is unrecoverable. `sqlite-sidecar-mcp` sits next to that application as one more SQLite client and
speaks MCP over HTTP. The owning application does not change.

It runs in production next to the [MCP Canary](https://mcpcanary.com) API, where it gives the
operator's coding agent read-only access to the live database.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    agent[AI / MCP client] -->|HTTPS| proxy[Reverse proxy]
    proxy -->|private HTTP| sidecar[sqlite-sidecar-mcp]
    sidecar -->|SQLite client| db[(app.db)]
    app[Owning application] -->|SQLite client| db
```

The product defends against two callers. One is an unauthorized client, which the token and the
request budget stop. The other is an **authorized client that makes a mistake**, and that one is the
unusual part: an agent with permission to write can still write the wrong thing. Structured writes,
a mandatory predicate, a row limit that counts cascades, and a per-minute write budget exist for it.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **One sidecar process serves one database.** The request budget, the write budget and the
> idempotency cache live in process memory. A second replica gives you two independent budgets and
> two independent caches, and nothing reports it. Do not scale this service. Run a second sidecar
> only for a *different* database or a *different* trust boundary.

### Built with

- .NET 10, ASP.NET Core
- Model Context Protocol over Streamable HTTP
- `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` with the bundled native SQLite
- [TOON](https://github.com/toon-format/toon) for row output, which costs fewer tokens than JSON

(back to top)

## Getting started

### Prerequisites

- Docker
- A SQLite database that **already exists**. The sidecar never creates one: creation would hide a
  wrong path and leave an empty database next to the real one.

### Run it

```bash
docker run -d --name sqlite-sidecar \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -v /srv/myapp/data:/data \
  -e SQLITE_SIDECAR_DB=/data/app.db \
  -e SQLITE_SIDECAR_TOKEN='' \
  -e SQLITE_SIDECAR_PERMISSIONS=schema,read \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
  ghcr.io/xakpc/sqlite-mcp-sidecar:latest
```

The mount must be **writable**, also for the read-only permission set above. SQLite opens the `-shm`
file read-write for a read-only connection to a WAL database, and a read-only mount fails in a way
that reads like a permission fault rather than a configuration mistake.

### Connect an agent

The endpoint is `/db/mcp` and the token goes in an `Authorization` header:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "app-database": {
      "url": "https://example.com/db/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <the token>" }
    }
  }
}
```

There is no OAuth. A client that insists on OAuth discovery finds no resource metadata on a `401`
and stops; the expected consumer is one agent that an operator configured with a static header.

### Generate a token and an environment block

```bash
dotnet run scripts/token.cs
```

It asks for the deployment shape, mints a token from a cryptographic random source, repairs a
permission set that would fail startup, and prints the block as `.env`, shell or compose.

(back to top)

## The eight tools

Which tools exist is decided by the permission set. A tool the deployment does not cover is absent
from `tools/list` — it does not appear and then fail.

| Tool | Needs | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema` | `schema` | Returns the DDL of the user tables, views and indexes. No row data, no internal `sqlite_%` objects, no file path. |
| `query` | `read` | Runs **one** caller-written read statement and returns rows as TOON, inside a row limit, a byte limit and a timeout. |
| `insert` | `write` | Inserts one row from a table name and a value map. The caller sends no SQL. |
| `update` | `write` | Updates rows matched by a structured filter. Needs a filter and a `maxRows`. |
| `delete` | `write` | Deletes rows matched by a structured filter. Needs a filter and a `maxRows`. |
| `backup` | `backup` | Copies the live database while the owning application keeps writing. Answers with a task; the client polls for the outcome. |
| `diagnostics` | `diagnostics` | Reports a fixed set of health values, including the journal mode and a `quick_check`. |
| `execute_write_sql` | `danger-raw-write` | Runs one caller-written `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE`. See [Security](#security) before you enable it. |

A `query` answers in TOON, which is a compact tabular text:

```text
rows[2]{id,status}:
  54,done
  41,failed

truncated: false
```

`truncated: true` means a limit stopped the read, not that the query failed.

### Structured writes

`update` and `delete` take a flat filter, never SQL. Every condition joins with `AND`; there is no
`or` and no nesting. A disjunction is one call per branch, and that is the tighter bound: each call
is pre-counted and limited on its own, while one `or` call would pool the blast radius of every
branch into a sing
